sections.description: The diagnostic journey in this case illustrates the critical challenge of distinguishing secondary thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) from primary causes or other hematologic emergencies, particularly when sepsis obscures the clinical picture. sections.section_title: Pathophysiology of Complement-Mediated HUS and Infectious Triggers
sections.description: Complement-mediated haemolytic uraemic syndrome (CM-HUS), historically referred to as atypical HUS, is fundamentally driven by the dysregulated activation of the alternative complement pathway. Under physiological conditions, this pathway serves as a critical line of defense against encapsulated bacteria through the generation of opsonins and membrane attack complexes. However, in CM-HUS, loss-of-function mutations or autoantibodies affecting regulatory proteins—such as Factor H, Factor I, Factor B, or membrane cofactor protein (CD46)—prevent the timely termination of complement activation. This unchecked cascade leads to excessive consumption of terminal complement components and the deposition of inflammatory mediators on vascular endothelium. sections.section_title: Therapeutic Strategy: Balancing Infection Control and Complement Blockade
sections.description: The management of complement-mediated haemolytic uraemic syndrome (CM-HUS) triggered by *Capnocytophaga canimorsus* bacteremia presents a distinct therapeutic challenge: the need to halt life-threatening thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) while simultaneously avoiding the exacerbation of an active bacterial infection. Terminal complement inhibition, specifically via eculizumab, is the definitive treatment for CM-HUS as it blocks the cleavage of C5, preventing the formation of the membrane attack complex (C5b-9) responsible for endothelial damage. However, this mechanism also compromises host defense against encapsulated organisms, including *Neisseria* species and *Capnocytophaga*, which rely heavily on complement-mediated lysis for clearance.
